noteBlocks.lede: Measure a thousand heights, weigh a crate of apples, or time the same run again and again, and the results pile up in the same shape: one hump in the middle, falling away evenly on both sides. This lesson is about that shape, the normal curve, and the figures that come with it.
can: Recognise a variable that is roughly normal, and one that is not
Sketch the curve with the mean at the centre and the standard deviations marked
Use the 68% and 95% figures to find ranges and rough percentages

noteBlocks.md: The heights of adult women, the masses of apples from one orchard and the errors in repeated measurements of one length all make the same shape when you plot a lot of them: most values sit near the middle, and fewer and fewer lie further out on either side. The smooth outline of that shape is the normal curve, often called the bell curve.

noteBlocks.alt: A smooth, symmetric bell-shaped curve over a horizontal axis. A dashed line runs from the peak down to the axis, labelled mean = median = mode. The two tails, each labelled, run closer and closer to the axis without meeting it.
noteBlocks.caption: Symmetric about the mean, highest at the mean, and tails that come closer and closer to the axis without touching it.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these is most likely to follow a normal distribution?

noteBlocks.caption: The same distribution drawn with wide classes, then with narrow ones: as the classes narrow, the steps become the curve.

noteBlocks.md: A histogram of many heights with wide classes looks like a staircase. Make the classes narrower and the steps get smaller, until the outline is the smooth curve. Each bar's area stands for the fraction of the data in its class, so the whole area under the curve is 1.

noteBlocks.prompt: What does the whole area under a normal curve stand for?
options: All of the data, a fraction of 1
The standard deviation of the data
noteBlocks.answer: All of the data, a fraction of 1
noteBlocks.explain: Each bar's area is the fraction of the data in its class, and all the fractions together make 1. That is why an area under the curve is a probability, which the next lesson uses.

noteBlocks.alt: Two curves side by side. On the left, heights: a symmetric bell with one dashed line at its peak, labelled peak and mean. On the right, incomes: a curve that rises steeply, peaks early and has a long tail to the right; one dashed line marks the peak and another, further right, the mean.
noteBlocks.caption: In the bell the peak and the mean are the same place. In a skewed shape like incomes, the long tail pulls the mean away.

noteBlocks.md: The normal curve is symmetric about its mean, so half of the data lies on each side. It is highest at the mean. Its tails come closer and closer to the axis without touching it, so very large or very small values can happen, just more and more rarely.

noteBlocks.title: Why the three averages agree
noteBlocks.md: The mode is where the curve is highest, which is the centre. The median cuts the area in half, and by symmetry the halves meet at the centre too. So for a normal distribution the mean, the median and the mode are the same number.

noteBlocks.prompt: The hand spans of the pupils in a year group are normally distributed with mean 20.5 cm. What is the median hand span, in centimetres?
noteBlocks.explain: The curve is symmetric about the mean, so the median, which cuts the area in half, is also 20.5 cm.

noteBlocks.text: Why so many things are normal

noteBlocks.md: A height is the sum of many small influences, each pushing a little up or a little down. The PhET Plinko board does the same with balls: every peg gives a small push left or right, and the bin a ball lands in adds up its pushes. With many rows, the bins fill into a bell.

noteBlocks.title: PhET: Plinko Probability
noteBlocks.attribution: Simulation by PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder, licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 (https://phet.colorado.edu)
noteBlocks.task: Open the Lab screen and set the binary probability to 0.5. Start with only 2 rows and drop a few hundred balls. Then add rows one at a time, up to the most the board allows, and drop a few thousand. Describe how the outline of the full bins changes as the rows increase.

noteBlocks.prompt: On the Plinko board, what happens to the outline of the bins as you add more rows?
options: It comes closer to a smooth, symmetric bell
It flattens, with every bin equally full
It leans over towards one side
noteBlocks.answer: It comes closer to a smooth, symmetric bell
noteBlocks.explain: Each extra row adds one more small push, left or right. The more pushes a ball's final bin adds up, the closer the bins come to the normal curve, with the middle bins fullest.

noteBlocks.text: Within one or two standard deviations

noteBlocks.alt: A normal curve with vertical lines at the mean μ and at one and two standard deviations either side. The bands hold 34.1% between the mean and one standard deviation on each side, 13.6% between one and two, and 2.3% in each tail beyond two. Brackets above mark about 68% within one standard deviation and about 95% within two.
noteBlocks.caption: The shares of a normal distribution: about 68% lies within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two.

noteBlocks.md: The standard deviation sets the width of the bell. About 68% of the values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, and about 95% within two. Almost all, about 99.7%, lie within three, so a value more than three standard deviations from the mean is very unusual.
Newborn babies' masses have mean 3.4 kg and standard deviation 0.5 kg. Two standard deviations is 1 kg, so about 95% of newborns weigh between 2.4 kg and 4.4 kg.

noteBlocks.prompt: The marks in a test are normally distributed with mean 55 and standard deviation 7. About 68% of the marks lie between 48 and what mark?
noteBlocks.explain: One standard deviation either side of the mean: $55 - 7 = 48$ and $55 + 7 = 62$.

noteBlocks.alt: A normal curve with the region to the right of μ + σ shaded and labelled about 16%.
noteBlocks.caption: Beyond one standard deviation on one side: half of the 32% outside, about 16%.

noteBlocks.md: Because the curve is symmetric, every share splits evenly about the mean. Half of the values lie above the mean. The 32% outside one standard deviation is shared by two tails, so about 16% lie above the mean plus one standard deviation. The 5% outside two gives about 2.5% in each tail; the exact share is 2.3%.

noteBlocks.prompt: Newborn babies' masses have mean 3.4 kg and standard deviation 0.5 kg. About what percentage of newborns weigh more than 4.4 kg?
noteBlocks.explain: 4.4 kg is two standard deviations above the mean. The 5% outside two standard deviations splits into two tails of about 2.5% each.

noteBlocks.why: A Northern Ireland teacher on the normal distribution for CCEA Further Mathematics. As you watch, sketch each curve you see and mark the mean under its peak.

noteBlocks.prompt: The lengths of a kind of fish are normally distributed with mean 30 cm and standard deviation 2.5 cm. About 95% of the fish are between what length and 35 cm?
noteBlocks.explain: About 95% lies within two standard deviations: $2 \times 2.5 = 5$, and $30 - 5 = 25$ cm.

noteBlocks.md:
Recognise the bell: symmetric, highest at the mean, with tails that never touch the axis.
The mean, median and mode are equal, and the whole area under the curve is 1.
About 68% lies within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two, 99.7% within three.
For one tail, halve what is outside: about 16% beyond one standard deviation, 2.5% beyond two.

No paper has yet set a question on the shape alone: it comes inside the normal question, where the mean and standard deviation are given and a sketch with the mean and the value under the axis made full marks far more likely in 2019. workedExamples.stem: The heights of adult women in a town are normally distributed with mean 164 cm and standard deviation 6 cm. Find the two heights between which about 95% of the women lie.

steps.working: About 95% lies within two standard deviations of the mean: $\mu \pm 2\sigma$.
steps.decision: Pick the multiple from the percentage before any arithmetic: 68% goes with one standard deviation, 95% with two.

options: About 95% of a normal distribution lies within two standard deviations of the mean
95 is close to 100, and doubling reaches it
The standard deviation is always doubled
whyMenu.explain: The figure comes from the curve itself: the bands within two standard deviations hold 95% of the area. Within one they hold 68%, so the multiple depends on the percentage asked for.

steps.decision: Two standard deviations is the distance from the mean to each end of the range.
Go that distance below the mean for the lower end.

steps.working: $164 + 12 = 176$ cm, so about 95% lie between 152 cm and 176 cm.
steps.decision: And the same distance above it for the upper end: the range is centred on the mean.

twin.stem: The lengths of the leaves on a hedge are normally distributed with mean 8.2 cm and standard deviation 0.9 cm. Find the lower of the two lengths between which about 95% of the leaves lie.

items.stem: Before the lesson, a check on earlier work. Two classes both have a mean mark of 60. Class A's marks have standard deviation 4 and class B's have standard deviation 12. What does that tell you?
items.skill: What a standard deviation measures (from the lesson on mean and standard deviation)

options.text: Class B's marks are more spread out
options.feedback: Yes: the standard deviation measures spread about the mean. In this lesson it sets the width of the bell.

options.text: Class B did better on average
options.feedback: Both means are 60, so neither did better on average. The larger standard deviation says class B's marks are more spread out.

options.text: Class A has more pupils
options.feedback: The standard deviation says nothing about how many pupils there are; it measures how spread out the marks are.

items.stem: Another check on earlier work. A set of data has mean 50 and standard deviation 5. Which value is two standard deviations above the mean?
items.skill: Stepping from the mean in standard deviations (from the lesson on mean and standard deviation)

options.feedback: Yes: two steps of 5 above 50. Ranges in this lesson are built the same way.
That is one standard deviation above the mean. Two steps of 5 reach 60.
That adds 2 rather than two standard deviations. Two steps of 5 above 50 reach 60.

items.stem: One more check on earlier work. What fraction of a set of data lies above its median?
items.skill: The median cuts the data in half (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.text: A half
options.feedback: Yes: the median is the middle value, with half the data on each side. On a symmetric curve it sits at the mean.

options.text: A quarter
options.feedback: A quarter lies above the upper quartile. The median has half of the data above it.

options.text: It depends on the mean
options.feedback: The median always has half the data on each side, whatever the mean is.

items.stem: Which statement is true of every normal distribution?
items.skill: The properties of the normal curve

options.text: The mean, the median and the mode are equal
options.feedback: Yes: the curve is symmetric about the mean and highest there, so all three averages sit at the centre.

options.text: The mean is larger than the median
options.feedback: That happens in a skewed distribution with a long upper tail, such as incomes. A normal curve is symmetric, so the two are equal.

options.text: The curve meets the axis three standard deviations from the mean
options.feedback: The tails come closer and closer to the axis but never meet it; beyond three standard deviations is very rare, not impossible.

items.stem: About what percentage of a normal distribution lies within two standard deviations of the mean?

options.feedback: Yes: about 95% within two standard deviations, and about 68% within one.
68% is the share within ONE standard deviation. Two standard deviations hold about 95%.
47.5% is the share between the mean and two standard deviations on ONE side. Both sides together hold about 95%.

items.stem: Masses are normally distributed with mean 200 g and standard deviation 10 g. Between which two masses do about 68% of them lie?
items.skill: A range centred on the mean

options.text: 190 g and 210 g
options.feedback: Yes: one standard deviation either side of the mean.

options.text: 200 g and 210 g
